From this it can be inferred that it was not without cause that Hollandus the son became such a great master, for he inherited, as it were, <term>secrets|original: *arcana*</term> from his entire family.

No one who cites anything from his writings pays attention to this fact; instead, everyone writes "Johannes Isacus Hollandus," which in my opinion is a mere confusion. ...work <note>original: *Operation*; in an alchemical context, this refers to the practical laboratory procedures or the "Great Work" itself</note> can be established; yet it is difficult enough for it to bear fruit, and there is no need to hide good books, for they are of little use even when they do their best, and must first overcome various difficulties <note>original: *difficultäten*</note> themselves. 

For example: Writing a good book is difficult in the first place, before there is someone who has the gift from **GOD** to write thoroughly; and when it has been written with truly good gifts, it is difficult again to ensure that **envious people** <note>original: *Neidhammel*; a colorful German term literally meaning "envy-rams," referring to those who begrudge others their success or knowledge</note>, like you and your kind, do not come upon it—those who, out of envy, lock it away for their entire lives and keep it under **arrest** <note>original: *Arreſt*; here used figuratively to describe the suppression or withholding of a manuscript</note>, so that it benefits neither themselves nor others. 

If it then escapes this danger, it meets difficulties again in reaching such people who are gifted enough to understand it; and even where they understand it, it is once again difficult to strike the mark; if the mark is hit, it is dangerous lest the **Devil** prevent it; and when finally all these obstacles are overcome, it then depends on whether it will help certain people despite their **unworthiness**. And how should it not go likewise for us powerless humans in our cultivation of the good, since it indeed...

...cultivation of the Almighty Lord **JESUS** went the same way, such that all His labor benefited only a very few. Thus, as previously mentioned, even when they are not suppressed, good books cannot accomplish much good; how much less so when one intends to hide them away and leave them to the moths and worms—creatures which are strange enough as it is. 

In contrast, there is an abundance of useless works hatched annually like harmful vermin. These appear under changed titles, but always play the same old tune <note>original: *Leyren*; literally "hurdy-gurdy," implying a repetitive, monotonous, or mechanical recitation of facts</note>: "so writes Hippocrates, Galen, Luther, Augustine, the *Body of Law* <note>original: *Corpus Juris*; the fundamental collection of Roman law</note>, etc." It is as if one could not read these authorities for oneself, but required a thousand foolish repeaters first. Furthermore, such people must even be honored as great Doctors and <term>Licentiates</term> <note>a high-level academic degree qualifying the holder to teach or practice law/medicine; here used sarcastically to describe those who buy their titles</note> because of their lousy citing and hundredfold copying of other people's books. 

Most of these authors would themselves be better off starting as true disciples and learning something substantial before they begin to teach. Most, however, reverse this order, rising immediately from their childish youth to the rank of Doctor or the highest teaching degree; and because they cannot earn it through proper talents <note>original: *Gaben*; literally "gifts," referring to natural intellectual or spiritual abilities</note>, they have themselves graduated for money

<meta>This page concludes the editor’s preface, continuing the critique of the academic and publishing world. The previous page discussed how unqualified individuals rise to high status through superficial citations of authorities like Hippocrates and Galen.</meta>

-># Preface.<-

...graduate, just as if common water could be passed off as magnificent wine through a false written testimony. This is beyond measure strange to hear, and yet it is in full swing—not only in the world at large, but even within Christendom—that such young greenhorns <note>original: *Benten*; a derogatory term for inexperienced students or freshmen</note> are granted degrees for money. Only a few years prior, these same individuals were still attending ordinary grammar schools; indeed, sometimes so little time has passed that the neighbors have only just seen them riding hobby-horses <note>original: *steckẽreiten*</note> with other boys or engaging in other childish games. From where, then, should the great art of acting as **Doctors** and writing extensive **Volumes** come to them so quickly, since by right this requires a special gift from God and many years of experience? 

And nevertheless, such lifeless and hollow <note>original: *Krafft- und Safftlose*; literally "powerless and sap-less," implying the books lack essential vital energy</note> books are written in heaps. Would to God that such works were held back, and instead, the works of those precious men—of whom barely one is noticed in fifty or a hundred years—were promoted with the greatest diligence. How long has it been since **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a revolutionary physician and alchemist</note> lived, and we still do not have his *Book of Herbs* <note>original: *Herbarium*</note>? Likewise, we still lack most of the works of the dear **Carrichter** <note>Bartholomäus Carrichter (c. 1510–1567), a prominent physician to the Imperial court</note>, etc. 

But those who willfully withhold such works are public thieves of the world’s heritage <note>original: *Welt-diebe*</note>, no matter who they may be. But enough of this; I herewith commend the reader to God's protection and the fulfillment of the Holy Spirit. 

Written in February 1667.

# On the Hand of the Philosophers.

This is the Hand of the Philosophers with its seven secret signs / with which hand the ancient sages bound and swore an oath to one another. No one can understand this hand with its secret signs / unless it be the case / that he first becomes an initiate <note>original: "geschworner" — one who has sworn a formal oath of secrecy</note> of the philosophers / and has faithfully served them in the art of Alchemy. Therefore / whoever does not have this hand / and does not understand its secret signs / nor has faithfully sworn an oath by it / such people are bastards in this art / they shall not possess the treasure of the philosophers. Therefore I advise all those / who do not have these secrets of the hand / that they do not set to work in the <term>alchemical art</term><note>Alchemy was viewed not just as chemistry, but as a spiritual and physical discipline to perfect matter and the soul.</note> / nor believe the books and writings / since they shall all be deceived regarding the secrets of the hand / therefore let everyone take good heed.

In this hand is enclosed the secret of the philosophers / namely of the <term>Seed and the Earth</term><note>In alchemical theory, the "Seed" usually refers to the active, masculine principle (often associated with sulfur) and the "Earth" refers to the receptive, feminine matrix or matter (mercury) in which the seed must grow.</note> / as shall be reported hereafter.

Now I will then teach my child / and describe the hidden secrets of the wise philosophers and masters of the true art of Alchemy, which no one can use / or

<margin>The Sun ☉</margin>

### 3. The Middle Finger.

<margin>✳</margin> The third sign of the Philosophical Hand is the Sun, standing above the third finger; by this, <term>Sal Ammoniac</term><note>original: "Salarmeniacum" — A volatile salt (ammonium chloride) used to dissolve metals and "spiritualize" solid matter.</note> is designated; for next to saltpeter and vitriol, one finds nothing more powerful than this; therefore it is the third secret.

### 4. The Ring Finger.

<margin>☉</margin> The fourth secret sign of the philosophers is the Lantern, standing over the fourth finger <note>original: "Goldfinger" — The ring finger, traditionally associated with the sun and gold.</note> of the hand, by which <term>Rock Alum</term><note>original: "Alumen roche" — A naturally occurring mineral salt used as a fixative and in the purification of chemicals.</note> is indicated; for without alum one can complete no perfect work, since one must have it for both the red and the white <note>The "Red" and "White" refer to the two stages of the Philosopher's Stone: the White Tincture (turning metals to silver) and the Red Tincture (turning metals to gold).</note>. It is of a wondrous nature and has the most subtle spirit <note>original: "spiritum"</note>; its nature is found described elsewhere.

### 5. The Little Finger.

<margin>⊝</margin> The fifth mystery and sign is the Key of the Philosophers, standing over the little finger <note>original: "Ohrfinger" — Literally "ear-finger," as it was the finger used to clean the ear.</note>, and it is at the same time the lock of the hand; therefore the key stands upon it, and by this coarse salt is designated; for salt is the key in this art.

### 6. The Palm of the Hand.

<margin>☿</margin> The sixth secret sign is the Fish, which stands in the middle of the hand and signifies Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>; for without Mercury or the fish, nothing can be done; it is the beginning, middle, and end, and is the priest who must marry all things.

# Preparation of the Coarse Salt or the Salt.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, ornate key. The bow of the key is heart-shaped with decorative protrusions on the sides, and the bit has a complex, multi-toothed pattern.</image-desc>

Take sea salt, pulverize it in a mortar, dissolve it in distilled white wine vinegar, filter it, and congeal <note>original: congelirs; to solidify a liquid into a crust or solid state</note> it until a small skin appears on top. Take that off and save it, for it is the **Spirit of the Key**. Dissolve and congeal it again until a skin appears on it; take that off once more, and thus the spirit is separated from the body <note>original: corpore; the physical, solid matter</note>. To 10 pounds of this spirit, add 1 pound of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: Salmiak; ammonium chloride, used as a flux in alchemy</note> and dissolve it in distilled rainwater. Coagulate it again using an alembic <note>a pear-shaped distilling vessel</note> along with a receiver, until it is coagulated. Then take it out and grind it upon a stone, and put your powder into a glass. Dissolve and coagulate it again until it is fixed <note>original: fix; meaning the substance has become stable under heat and will no longer vaporize</note> and no longer rises. With this spirit, one performs many wonders and miraculous works within the metals, and especially with Mercury, <term>Tin</term> <note>original symbol: ♃ (Jupiter)</note> and <term>Lead</term> <note>original symbol: ♄ (Saturn)</note>. However, this spirit must first be prepared as I shall yet teach.

...the greatest error occurs among all people who practice the Art, because the greatest mystery and secrets <note>original: secreta; hidden properties or recipes</note> lie in salts. Therefore, understand well what I shall teach here: for just as you separate the spirit <note>original: spiritum; the volatile, active essence</note> from the body of coarse salt, so one separates the spirit from the body <note>original: corpore; the solid, material remains</note> of all other things. However, they are not all prepared in the same way, but each according to its function, according to what is needed, and according to how one intends to work with it.

There are many kinds of preparations of salts <note>original: salien</note>, for the entire Art of Alchemy <note>original: Alchymi</note> consists in the power of salts and their preparation <note>original: præparation</note>. One can work with no salt unless the spirit is first separated from the body; then the spirit must be prepared according to the work that requires it. Likewise, the body <note>original: corpus</note> must also be prepared for other works, for the spirit and the body each have their own distinct power and perform opposing effects, just as they are contrary <note>original: contrari</note> to one another. Once they are separated, they perform opposing operations <note>original: operationes</note>, each in its own realm. 

Those who wish to operate with unseparated salts will find all their efforts to be wasted labor; they deceive themselves and everyone who believes them. They will also reach no perfection <note>original: perfection; the completion or "ripening" of the alchemical Work</note>, for the entire Art is the separation of the Salt and the preparation of the Sulfur <note>original: Sulphuris</note>. For there are various salts, and likewise various preparations, and the same is true for Sulfur and its preparation, according to how the...

...works are. The fools who read about Sulphur in our books are of the opinion that we speak of the <term>common mineral</term> <note>original: ♁; while this symbol often denotes Antimony, the author clarifies it refers here to the crude yellow sulfur dug from the earth</note> which is dug out of the earth; but we all mean a different sulphur. There are not so many varieties of salts <note>original: salien</note> that there should not also be just as many sulphurs and their preparations; and one must make the sulphur artificially, just as one makes <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: ⚹; ammonium chloride</note> artificially. Now we will return to our material. First, I have taught you to separate the spirit <note>original: spiritum; the volatile essence</note> and the body <note>original: corpus; the solid matter</note> from one another; now I will instruct you on how to prepare the spirit and make it fixed <note>original: fix; to make a substance resistant to evaporation or change when heated</note>, as well as what you should do with it.

Once you have removed the little skin <note>original: Häutlein; a film or crust forming on the surface during the process</note>, which is the spirit of the salt, and have collected as much of it as you could, dissolve it again in distilled rainwater in which you dissolved your salt. Then congeal <note>original: congelirs; to solidify a liquid into a salt or crust</note> it again in a glass or glass vessel over a gentle fire. Pulverize it in a stone mortar, and also add powdered <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: ⚹</note> to it. Mix them well together and place it in a glass with a long neck. Seal it <note>original: lutirs; to apply "lute," a clay-like paste used to make laboratory joints airtight</note> diligently, then place it in horse manure <note>original: Pferdsmist; used by alchemists as a natural, low-temperature heating pad for gentle digestion</note> or in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: balneū / balneum</note> to dissolve. The glass must be well-stopped at the top, or place a <term>still-head</term> <note>original: Helm; the "helmet" or cap of a distilling apparatus</note> over it and a <term>receiver</term> <note>original: Recipienten; a vessel to catch condensed vapors</note> attached to it, everything well-sealed. In case any moisture should come over, if an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: alembicus; a specialized distillation vessel</note> is on top, it will coagulate all the more easily than if it were only poorly stopped. This dissolving and congealing in a water bath or horse manure must be repeated 10 or 12 times, or more, until it is fixed.

## To Bring All Metals to Water

Now we wish to teach you how to bring all metals to water, since they must altogether first become water before they can be brought to <term>perfection</term> <note>The state of being transmuted into the "perfect" metals, gold or silver.</note>. Now, make the <term>mercury</term> <note>original: ☿</note> clean of its "blackness" <note>The "blackness" or *nigredo* refers to the initial state of matter, full of impurities that must be purged.</note> and purify it well without vinegar; then dissolve it again in the aforementioned water. Then you may dissolve in it whichever metal you wish to work with. And when it is dissolved, then take sweet, fresh <term>whey</term> <note>original: Keßmatten; the liquid remaining after milk has been curdled and the solids removed</note>, boil it and skim off the thick matter, and let it settle. Separate what remains clear and pour a little of it into that which you have dissolved; thus it will <term>precipitate</term> <note>original: præcipitiren</note> into a <term>mass</term> <note>original: massa</note>. Separate the water from the mass; then you may purify it of its blackness with salt and vinegar, and continue working toward whatever you desire the metals to become—to the red or to the white <note>The "red" refers to the work for gold (rubedo), and the "white" refers to the work for silver (albedo).</note>—as the works shall demonstrate. But all metals must be water and purified of their blackness if they are to be brought to perfection; or the <term>Great Elixir</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy.</note> must do it, for that has the power and nothing else.

[sul]phur prepare. Understand me well: I will teach you about the **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"</note>, with which you must make the **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> healthy; and by way of this sulfur, I will teach you how to make all other sulfurs.

Mercury is cold and moist in its outward nature, and in its innermost part it is hot and dry. ### Another Coagulation of Mercury

Take <note>represented by the symbol ℞, the standard medical and alchemical abbreviation for "recipe"</note> one pound [℔] of roche alum <note>original: "alumen roche." Literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid.</note> and place four pig galls into the receiving vessel. Pour this *Aqua Fortis* onto mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> in a glazed pot over warm sand or ashes until the mercury is congealed.

Put this congealed mercury into a glass and add half a pound of lead to it; melt them together. Meanwhile, have two pounds of melted lead <note>original: "Saturnū." Then, have ready a long-necked pot or a Siegburg jug <note>original: "Syburgische Kanne." A famous type of salt-glazed stoneware from the Rhineland.</note>, well-sealed with luting-clay <note>original: "verlutirt." Put into it pitch, resin, sulfur <note>represented by the symbol 🜍</note>, human hair, horn, sliced cow hooves, and one pound of pig dung. Add four ounces each of nard oil <note>original: "Nardenöhl." An aromatic essential oil.</note> and linseed oil. Melt everything together in the jug. When it is melted, put it into a crucible; then pour the melted lead and mercury into it and plug it immediately so that the flame does not strike out. Let it stand in the heat for 24 hours. When it is cold, take it out and refine it on a cupel; thus you will have fine gold <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note> in all tests.

### The Operation of Tartar <note>original: "Operatio tartari"</note>, or of Cream of Tartar.

Thus one prepares the tartar <note>original: "tartarum"</note>, and this is very good, and it contains the four elements within it, but not like other things, <term>species<note>referring to specific alchemical or medicinal ingredients</note></term>, and herbs.

In all things that God the Almighty has created from the four elements, the elements within are soiled and impure; such things cannot be purified except through <term>distilling</term>, <term>sublimating<note>heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again to purify it</note></term>, <term>calcinating<note>heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts or achieve oxidation</note></term>, <term>cementing<note>a high-heat process used to purify metals by surrounding them with a powdered agent</note></term>, etc. In this manner, one can make the elements pure through great labor. One finds nothing in the world that is quite like tartar <note>original: "Weinstein"; literally "wine-stone," the crystalline crust found in wine barrels</note>, for God has left no impurity within it, since it separates itself from the wine as water does from fire; and the tartar takes no impurity from the wine, just as water likewise takes none from the fire; instead, if there is impurity in the water, it will leave <note>original: "las-"; catchword for "lassen," meaning to leave or abandon</note> those same impurities behind in the fire—

...leave [them], so that the fire might burn them and reduce them to nothing; for the fire consumes all impurity, and with fire one must cleanse all the impurities of the elements. Nevertheless, fire is fragile in itself, namely in that it is not fixed <note>original: "fix"; in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can endure high heat without evaporating or being destroyed</note>; for when God corrupted the four elements, He corrupted the fire along with them; therefore, ordinary fire is not fixed.

But tartar <note>original: "tartarus"; the potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine barrels, highly valued by alchemists</note> is a fire without air and without flame, fixed and pure; therefore, no one can separate the element from the tartar, since it is a glorified body <note>original: "glorificirt corpus"; a spiritualized or perfected physical form</note>. Nothing can destroy tartar, nor can fire burn it. Cream of tartar <note>original: "Weinstein"; literally "wine-stone"</note> is the fixed fire about which we often write in our books. If fire has the power to cleanse all corrupted elements, and to burn and consume all impurities, and also to make all other elements fixed, and since this [tartar] is a "fire above fire," what might it do when it enters into the impure elements? 

Truly, I tell you: tartar has the power to make all our things fixed when it is prepared, and within it lie all hidden things, which would take too long to describe. However, one cannot complete any perfect work in the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy</note> without tartar, nor can the hand be prepared without tartar; for if tartar did not exist, the Art would be false. Thus, tartar is the Master of Alchemy; for this reason, the masters regard it as their fixed fire, which burns away everything that is not fixed, etc.

Take good white tartar from good Rhenish wine; wash the powder clean until the water runs clear from it, and let this be done with clear spring water. Then dry it in the sun. Grind it small on a stone with good distilled wine vinegar and dry it in the sun; then moisten it again on the stone with fresh vinegar until it is like a thick paste and dry it once more. Do this at least 10 times or more. This thus-imbibed <term>tartar <note>original: "tartarum"; the crude crust from wine vats, processed here to become a powerful alchemical agent</note></term> place into a strong and suitable vessel and seal it very firmly, perhaps a hand’s breadth thick. 

Then take another, even larger vessel and fill it with quicklime <note>original: "lebendigem Kalck"; calcium oxide, which generates intense heat when reacting</note>; place the vessel containing the tartar inside it, and then fill the large vessel completely with quicklime around the tartar, so that it lies in the middle like a yolk in an egg. Then seal this also very firmly with lute <note>original: "lutir"; a clay or airtight paste used to seal alchemical equipment</note>, as strongly as you can, a large hand’s breadth thick, and let it all dry gently on its own. 

In your hearth, where you keep a daily fire, make a large hole; fill it with quicklime, place the vessel inside, and fill it all around with quicklime, but leave the belly of the vessel exposed. Upon this, burn your fire for 8 weeks, and keep it hot day and night; afterward in a glowing heat—the more it is calcined <note>original: "calcinirt"; reduced to a powder through prolonged high heat</note>, the better. Following this, carefully take the small vessel out of the lime, break it open, and pour the tartar into a large quantity of distilled vinegar. Let it settle or become clear for 3 days; pour off the clear liquid from the top into another vessel,

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the three treatises by Isaac Hollandus. ...[and] applies it well to the honor of God and the needs of his neighbor.

The second kind of alchemy is the **Elixir**, which is prepared as the ancients taught, from the **Hand of the Philosophers**; those who possess this and understand it well may also be called blessed.

The third kind is the **Irir** <note>original: "Irir"; a term used here to denote a specific alchemical category or substance, possibly related to the "Iris" or rainbow stage of the work, though distinct from the Great Elixir</note>, and it is also an art of the old and wise masters of the Hand; and whoever can prepare such as the fathers prepared it and left it to us, will likewise reign in joy in this world.

The art of alchemy has many more daughters, branches, and roots, which sprout from these three trees I have just mentioned; that is: that some labor with great effort in the <term>calcination <note>original: "calciniren"; heating a substance to a high temperature to remove volatile parts or reduce it to a powder</note></term> of <term>bodies <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" almost always refers to the seven base metals</note></term>, in order to wash them and make them pure and clean. ## The Third Kind of Alchemy
### Called Ixir.

Now I will continue with a few words to mention the **Ixir**, which is the third part upon which Alchemy stands, as I mentioned at the beginning of this book. You should know that one may well make an **Ixir** from our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance sought by alchemists to enable transmutation.</note>; for where the **soul, spirit, and body** <note>In alchemical theory, these refer to the three principles of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt which must be harmonized.</note> are not joined together as they should be, and are also not **fixed** <note>original: figiret; to 'fix' a substance in alchemy means to make it stable under heat so it does not evaporate or change state unexpectedly.</note> with one another—all such things which are not perfected are called **Ixirs**.

But where soul, body, and spirit are joined together as is fitting, and fixed with one another and also made **fusible** <note>Capable of being melted or liquified by heat.</note>—those are all **Elixirs** and good for eternity. And the **Elixir** transmutates all impure metals into fine **Gold** and **Silver** without any help from other things. But I advise you that you perform no **projection** <note>The final step of the alchemical process, where the transformative powder is 'projected' or thrown onto a molten base metal.</note> upon **Copper** <term>♀</term> with an Elixir, but rather take the most beautiful and yellow **brass**; for then your Elixir will perform a much higher projection than it would upon **Tin** <term>♃</term> or red **Copper** <term>♀</term>; also more beautiful,

### Preface to the Work of Saturn.

Although, beloved reader, the noble little book by Hollandus called the **Work of Saturn** <note>original: "opus Saturni"</note> is to be found printed within Basilius Valentinus’s *Triumphal Chariot* <note>Referring to the famous alchemical text "The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony."</note>, I nevertheless wished to include it with these writings of his for several reasons. First, because Hollandus himself writes therein that this work of his belongs not to the **Mineral Work** <note>original: "Opere Minerali"</note>, but to the **Vegetable Work** <note>original: "Opere Vegetabili." In alchemy, the "Vegetable Work" refers to the "vegetable kingdom" or organic matter, believed to hold different transformative properties than minerals.</note>, and is the beginning and principal part of the Vegetable book. He also cites in this **Work of Saturn** his vegetable writings which follow hereafter; it seems to me, therefore, not improper that they should follow one after another here, so that one may explain the other and they may be compared side-by-side.

Furthermore, the version of the **Work of Saturn** already in print was translated very much according to the **Dutch idiom** <note>original: "Niederländischen redart." At this time, Dutch and Low German were often closely grouped.</note>, which at times uses words or phrases unintelligible to High Germans. I have therefore endeavored to translate various parts more clearly for the High German reader, adapting the text to the **High German** style of speech while nevertheless taking care not to deviate from the author’s meaning and intention.

You should also be informed that in the **Low German** <note>original: "Niederdeutschen"</note> manuscript, I likewise found no division of chapters, just as it was maintained in the aforementioned printed version. I have, however, nonetheless arranged it into certain **chapters** <note>original: "capita"</note> so that the contents may be more easily held in memory, just as also...

<summary>In this preface, the translator explains that they have included Hollandus's "Work of Saturn" because it serves as an essential introduction to his "Vegetable Work." The translator also notes that they have updated the language from Dutch/Low German to High German and added chapter divisions for better readability.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Work of Saturn, Johannes Isacus Hollandus, Basilius Valentinus, Vegetable Work, Mineral Work, High German, translation style, chapter divisions</keywords>

...such division of the chapters can serve the purpose that, whenever one wishes to cite or take note of something from it, this may be done all the more quickly and easily by specifying the chapter. Beyond this, it is also to be noted that whatever appears between such signs <note>original: "signis"</note> [ ] are not the author's <note>original: "Authoris"</note> words, but rather those of the translator, which have been included with good intentions so that certain obscure words <note>original: "dunckele Wörter." In alchemical literature, "dark" or "obscure" words often refer to "Decknamen" (cover-names) or archaic terms that the translator is attempting to clarify for the reader.</note> might be better understood. 

With this, fare thee well.

# Chapter 2.

My child, lock this into your heart and understanding: namely, that this very same Saturn <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for the metal lead</term> is the selfsame Stone which the philosophers did not wish to make known by name. Therefore, its name has remained hidden until this very day; for if the name were known, there would be many who would wish to work with it, and the Art <term>the Art: Alchemy, often called the "Royal Art" or "Great Work"</term> would become common. This is because its work is short, inexpensive, and requires only a small and slight amount of labor. For this reason, the name has remained hidden because of the evil that might arise from it <note>Alchemists often believed that if the secret of making gold became common, it would lead to economic collapse or moral corruption</note>. 

All the wondrous parables which the philosophers have spoken in a veiled manner concerning a stone, a poppy <note>original: "Mohn"; while this literally means poppy, it often serves as an alchemical metaphor for the "sleep" of the metal or its transformation</note>, a furnace, or a vessel—all of these are Saturn. Therefore, no one in the world is so poor that they would not be able to work upon and continue this labor; for in a short time, one may indeed make Luna <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term> out of Saturn with easy labor. If it is sweet, then it is not yet sufficiently dissolved (as long as the added vinegar still becomes sweet); or take a little (of the most recently added vinegar that has stood on it for a while) into a small glass bowl, and let it *evaporate* <term>evaporiren: to drive off liquid by heat, leaving behind solid matter</term>. Then *congeal* it <term>congeliren: to thicken or crystallize a substance</term> as before; then pour fresh vinegar on it again and stir it once more (with the spoon), and place it in the water bath. ### Chapter 17.

<margin>Multiplication of the Tincture.</margin>

How, then, my child, you should multiply the Stone: take ten times as much prepared Saturn <term>Saturn: The alchemical name for lead, which this author considers the primary material for the Great Work</term>, as I have taught you above (how to prepare it) through congealing and dissolving <term>congealing and dissolving: the repetitive process of solidifying and liquefying a substance to purify it of impurities</term> until it leaves no dregs <note>original: *feces*</note> behind. Then take your precious red powder out of the glass (taking one part of this powder for every ten parts of prepared Saturn <note>original: *Saturni præparati*</note>); mix it into the Saturn, put them together into a glass vessel, and pour distilled wine vinegar onto it—enough so that two-thirds of the glass is full. Place it in your warm water bath <term>water bath: also known as a *balneum Mariae*, a vessel used for gentle, indirect heating, similar to a double boiler</term> and let it dissolve. Once a portion has dissolved, pour off the clear liquid from the top into another glass, pour more fresh vinegar onto the remainder, and let it dissolve as before.

Continue this process of pouring off and adding fresh vinegar until everything has dissolved into clear water; this usually happens quickly, perhaps in 10 or 12 days. Then place all the dissolved liquid into the water bath, put a distilling lid <note>original: *Helm*; an alembic head used for capturing vapors</note> on it, and distill all the vinegar away from it again. Congeal the material until it appears completely dry. Then take it out of that glass and put it into another fixing-glass; place it on a furnace in a container <term>container: a *test*, often a shallow vessel or cupel used in metalworking</term> filled with sifted ashes, and place a small polished piece of glass over the mouth of the vessel (weighted down with a leaden weight, so that by the weight it is pressed more firmly and tightly onto the mouth). My child must know that your material (the ten parts of the prepared Saturn) has already become fixed <term>fixed: in alchemy, to "fix" a substance means to make it stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates or changes state</term> during the solution <note>original: *solution*; the process of dissolving</note> with the Stone.

You shall investigate it in this manner: take a little of the powder out of the glass, lay it upon a glowing silver plate, and if it melts like wax and penetrates through the plate <term>plate: original *Lamel*, a thin sheet of metal</term> as oil through dry leather, and turns it through and through into gold as far as the powder has reached, then the Stone is finished; but if it does not yet do so, you must let it stand in the same heat until it performs this without smoking.

### Chapter 22.

<margin>The use of the Stone upon the metals.</margin>
My child, take to heart how and in what manner one should use this Stone. At that stage, it is still all medicine <term>medicin: a potent alchemical substance that can be further multiplied or used for healing purposes</term>. Then cast one part of those 1,000 parts upon ten parts [of base metal], and it will become the best gold that has ever been seen on earth.

# Preface of the Translator to the *Opus Vegetabile* <note>original: "opus Vegetabile"; this refers to the "Vegetable Work," a treatise on the alchemical properties and tinctures derived from the plant kingdom.</note>.

Friendly and much-beloved reader, I have no doubt that it is well known to you and all lovers of the secrets of nature how intensely, for a long time now—indeed, doubtless from the time when some of his writings first came to light, whether during the lifetime of Hollandus <note>Referring to Johann Isaac Hollandus or his son, legendary 15th-century Dutch alchemists whose works were widely circulated in the 17th century.</note> or soon after his death—people have sought after the unpublished works of the well-regarded Hollandus. This is especially true of his *Opus Vegetabile*, which he himself cited everywhere, so much so that enthusiasts can be found here and there who let it be known that they would pay large sums of money for such a "vegetable work" if they could only get hold of it. Everyone is under the firm impression that nothing of this work has yet been made public, but rather that it has either already been lost or is perhaps being withheld by envious people <note>The "envious" or "jealous" man is a common alchemical trope referring to those who hoard secret knowledge rather than sharing it with the worthy.</note>. I myself was always of this opinion, not believing that anything of it would ever be seen. However, because I nevertheless continued to search for it and for other things he wrote, some very rare items of his have come into my hands—just as I recently [found] the third part of the *Opus Mineralis* <note>original: "Operis Mineralis"; the "Mineral Work," focusing on metals and stones.</note>, of which I myself had never heard before...

<summary>In this preface, the translator describes the legendary status of the alchemist Hollandus and the intense desire among scholars to find his "lost" manuscript on plant alchemy. The translator reveals that after much searching, they have successfully recovered several rare texts, including parts of the "Mineral Work" and the "Vegetable Work."</summary>

He states that this <term>Opus Saturni</term> is the most important part and the very beginning of the <term>Opus Vegetabile</term>. From this, we can conclude that Hollandus had incorporated the <term>Opus Saturni</term>, along with other fine treatises, into the <term>Opus Vegetabile</term>, organizing the entire work into a structure and chapters that pleased him,

...about which later, perhaps, ignorant people might encounter them—people who did not observe the order maintained by Hollandus <note>original: "Hollandi"; referring to the famous alchemical family Isaac and John Isaac Hollandus.</note>, but instead one person copied this and another copied that. In this manner, the treatises were taken out of their proper order and scattered. Thus, it is undoubtedly true that while the treatises still exist here and there in a scattered state, it is difficult for anyone to know the sequence in which they should follow one another. Few people even concern themselves with this, being satisfied as long as they have whatever suits their own temperament <note>original: "Humeur"; referring to the reader's personal interest or disposition.</note>. Consequently, such confusion is now easier to lament than it is to set right again. 

However, it is still a good thing that the treatises belonging to this *Vegetable Work* <note>original: "Opus Vegetabile"</note> are gradually being recovered, and enough are already present that one can find their way through them reasonably well. And because one treatise always cites another, it is to be hoped that the proper order will eventually be discovered from them, as well as which specific treatises are still missing. ### Chapter 2.

My child, let it be known to you that this **Divine Medicine** <term>Divine Medicine</term> <note>original: "Göttliche Medicin"; in alchemy, this refers to the Philosopher's Stone or the Universal Elixir, capable of perfecting both metals and the human body.</note> consists of three types of knowledge and three manual crafts, and they have three distinct names, which are nonetheless all one; just as the **Holy Trinity** <note>The author uses the central Christian mystery of the Trinity as a pedagogical analogy to explain how one substance can manifest in three distinct forms or kingdoms without losing its essential unity.</note> consists of three distinct persons, who indeed have three distinct names, such as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit; likewise, the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but each is a distinct person, and yet these three distinct persons are one being, and in one power and one strength.

So it is also with these three different medicines: one is not the other, and although they are three different kinds, they are nonetheless one in essence, and of equal nature and power, with three different names: **Vegetable** <term>Vegetable</term>, **Animal** <term>Animal</term>, and **Mineral** <term>Mineral</term>.

Under the **Vegetable** <note>original: "Vegetabilisch"</note> you must understand everything that grows out of the earth, such as herbs, trees, spices, fruits, and everything that sprouts out of the earth such as roots, flowers, and the like.

### Chapter 36.

# The Second Treatise of the Vegetable Work.

### Here begins the second manner of working in the Vegetable Work, namely where the cloud-water or phlegm comes over first.

### Chapter 1.

Now you shall learn the second method, specifically regarding those herbs where the water comes over first. For under this method, all kinds of herbs are to be understood in which the <term>cloud-water <note>original: "Wolckenwasser"; the first watery, clear distillate that rises during the heating of plant matter, often called "phlegm."</note></term> rises first. Through this practical work and the teachings contained within it, you will understand everything that is to be done with green herbs. Afterward, however, the third method will also be taught, namely concerning all dry species, such as woods, gums, and so forth—everything that is dry—each with its own instruction on how and in what form it must be thus and not otherwise.

# Preface

After this precious little book came into my hands while inquiring into the writings of famous persons, along with a written report stating that it came from the "Glassbergers" <note>This likely refers to individuals from Szklana Góra (Glass Mountain) or a specific family/group associated with the Polish nobility.</note> of the former servant of the Polish Lord Cortiski, which he received together with the mass <note>original: "una cum massa"</note> (by which I understand a certain portion of the tincture <note>original: "portione quadam tincturæ"</note>) from Mr. Johann Porroski, the servant of Mr. Michael Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a world-renowned Polish alchemist and pioneer of chemistry who discovered that air contains a "food of life."</note>; I have not withheld this from the seekers of truth. Instead, I wished to promote its printing alongside the writings of Hollandus <note>Referring to Isaac Hollandus or John Isaac Hollandus, influential alchemists whose works focused on practical laboratory operations.</note>, believing that these two leaders of the **Hermetic Art** <term>Hermetic Art</term> <note>The tradition of alchemy and natural philosophy named after the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note> are not ill-suited to one another. One of them [Hollandus] describes the rarest practical techniques that may occur in the entire **Chemical Art** <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Chymistry" encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the spiritual/transmutational goals of alchemy.</note>, while the other [Sendivogius] provides the clearest description of the **second matter** <note>original: "materia secunda"; in alchemy, this is the raw material of the world after it has been partially processed by nature or the artist.</note> or the **seed of things** <note>original: "spermatis rerum"; the invisible life-force or "sperm" that allows minerals and metals to grow within the earth.</note> better than all other philosophers.

And I consider this little treatise every bit as necessary and useful as his—namely Mr. Sendivogius's—still-promised writings, namely on **Philosophical Salt** and **Harmony**; indeed, this work may in a pinch fill the lack of them, especially regarding the **generation** <note>The natural process of birth or creation.</note> and **regeneration** of metals, as these subjects are presented here so brightly and clearly that I would not know how it

->Chapter I.<-

### The First Error of Presumed Alchemists
### in the Reading of False Books and the Teaching
### of the Magnificent Art.

Since it has now come to pass, in the current state of this world, that almost all persons of high and low station—for the sake of vain, perishable splendor and luxury—set aside their rank and profession to desire to learn and experience the **Art of Alchemy** <note>original: "Chymiam"</note>, in order to obtain and acquire great, excessive wealth; seeing as this Art, above all other arts, trades, and businesses, promises and pledges such great and overwhelming riches; and likewise because the whole world is filled with books (mostly indeed fabricated by deceivers) concerning this Art and its calculation, wherein the strangest and most wonderful works and **recipes** <note>original: "recepte"</note> of this Art are described; hence it follows that when these books are read by men greedy for wealth, or when they are told of their contents by others, they immediately believe they can learn from them how to make the Art of <term>gold</term> <note>symbol: ☉</note> and <term>silver</term> <note>symbol: ☾</note> by weight in a flash <note>original: "in einem Hui." A German idiom meaning instantly or in the blink of an eye.</note>; for since, according to the appearance of said books, this Art is quite easy and to be accomplished in a short time, everyone thinks of how he might soon come into such great wealth.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metallic generation, transitioning from the formation of Tin (from vitriolic and aluminous salts) to the specific composition of Iron. The catchword "Dem" from the previous page likely began a phrase such as "Demnach man..." (Accordingly, one...)</meta>

...[Accordingly, one] can forge good **iron**. This occurs because all earth—whether it be fertile or infertile—contains a hidden **salt** within itself that is mixed with a small amount of combustible <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: "Sulphur"; in alchemical theory, sulfur was the principle of combustibility and fluidity.</note>. This salt is then mixed with the rising water and is gradually <term>coagulated</term> <note>original: "coaguliret"; the process of thickening or solidifying from a liquid state.</note> by the air at the surface and mingled with the coarse earth.

However, that which is generated in the earth and in the ore—which is called <term>ironstone</term> <note>original: "Eisenstein"; raw iron ore.</note>—comes about through the mixing of the <term>vitriolic salt</term> <note>original: "Vitriolischen Saltz"; sulfate minerals which alchemists believed gave iron its specific "sharp" and hardy character.</note> found in those places in the earth. Because this vitriol carries more sulfur with it than other salts, it becomes hard within the earth and coagulates into ironstone. When it is processed through the **smelting furnace**, it reveals itself as iron, though it loses most of its sulfur in the heat. 

Because the sulfur has escaped it, the iron is thereafter more difficult to melt than any other metal; for its remaining <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus"; the physical substance of the metal after its "spirituous" components have been driven off.</note> consists only of sharp vitriolic salt and earth. This is also why it **rusts** so quickly in water or moisture: as the salt is gradually <term>resolved</term> <note>original: "resolviret"; dissolved or broken down into its constituent parts.</note>, the metal turns back into earth. The <term>lover of the art</term> <note>original: "kunstliebend"; a common address to a student of alchemy or metallurgy.</note> will know this and must observe it with diligence, for all easily melted metals possess their "easy flow" from sulfur alone. 

Therefore, if one heats **iron** or **steel** until it glows and throws common combustible sulfur upon it, it flows like **lead**. But because sulfur is combustible and cannot remain with the metal for long, this "flow" cannot last; as soon as the sulfur has burned away, the metal becomes as difficult to melt as it was before. This is indicated to the lovers of the art only as a simple test by way of analogy.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical composition of iron, attributing its hardness and tendency to rust to a combination of vitriolic salt and earth, while noting that its difficulty to melt is due to a lack of sulfur.</summary>

This he must pour for the third time over the **dregs** <note>original: *feces*; the solid residue remaining after distillation.</note> and distill from it again; thus, the longer it continues, the more beautiful and heavier it becomes. This same water he must seal well in a fresh glass and again **digest** in moist heat for 8 days. Afterward, with a very gentle **bath** <note>original: *balneo*; likely a *balneum Mariae* or water bath used for gentle, uniform heating.</note>, he should draw off some of the **phlegm** <note>The watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a distilled substance.</note>. Then he has at the bottom <note>original: *in fundo*</note> the most beautiful, clearest **sky-colored water**, heavy in weight, which
